analysis.one_liner: Eliminates the federal estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax entirely.
analysis.headline: Strom Thurmond's bill to repeal the estate tax drew no cosponsors, never got a hearing in the Senate Finance Committee, and died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have deleted the entire section of the tax code covering the estate tax (paid when someone dies and leaves wealth), the gift tax (paid on large lifetime gifts), and the generation-skipping transfer tax (paid when wealth jumps straight to grandchildren). It applied to everyone who died or made gifts after it became law. The bill never moved past being assigned to the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs of the largest estates. In 1996 the estate tax only applied to estates above roughly $600,000, so the benefit of full repeal would flow almost entirely to families with the largest wealth. Heirs would pay nothing on inheritances, and wealthy families would no longer need estate-planning workarounds.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the federal estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax outright by striking Subtitle B of the Internal Revenue Code, effective for deaths and gifts after enactment.
The bill's own findings argue that family-owned businesses and farms are hit hardest by estate taxes and that some are forced to liquidate to pay the bill, which repeal would stop.
The bill's findings note that estate and gift taxes raised only about 1 percent of federal receipts in fiscal year 1995, arguing repeal would cost the government little while spurring investment.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. Repealing a tax that raised roughly 1 percent of federal revenue means either the money is made up through other taxes, larger deficits, or reduced spending — costs spread across everyone, while the direct benefit concentrates in the largest estates.

drawbacks.text: Repeal eliminates a tax that falls almost exclusively on very large estates — the threshold in 1996 was roughly $600,000 — so the benefit would go to the wealthiest families while the lost revenue must be covered by other taxpayers, other taxes, or higher deficits.

The estate tax is one of the few parts of the code that taxes accumulated wealth directly; repealing it, as the bill would, removes that check on the growth of inherited fortunes and can concentrate wealth across generations, which is why the generation-skipping transfer tax exists.

Even by the bill's own account, estate and gift taxes were a real revenue source (1 percent of federal receipts in FY1995); the bill offers no replacement revenue, so repeal is a net loss to the Treasury.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit goes to a narrow group — heirs of estates above the roughly $600,000 exemption — while the cost, about 1 percent of federal revenue, is spread across everyone else through other taxes or larger deficits. The bill's arguments about protecting family farms and businesses describe a real concern, but full repeal goes far beyond what targeted relief for small estates would address. As designed, the bill is a large tax cut for the wealthiest families.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Strom Thurmond introduced the Estate and Gift Taxes Repeal Act of 1996 on September 13, 1996, less than two months before the end of the 104th Congress.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and no further action was ever recorded.
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and expired when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes remained in place, preserving roughly 1 percent of federal revenue that would otherwise have been lost — mostly paid by the largest estates. Heirs of large estates are worse off; ordinary taxpayers are unchanged.

for.name: Sen. Strom Thurmond
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to repeal the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes and delivered introductory remarks.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: The committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its referral; no hearing, markup, or committee vote was ever held.

against.name: 0 of 100 senators
against.what_they_did: None of the other 99 senators signed on as cosponsors during the bill's brief life.

sides.party_line_note: With a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, the bill never drew enough support to reveal a partisan pattern; it was an isolated proposal.

industries.industry: Heirs of the largest estates and wealthy families
industries.note: Full repeal would exempt inheritances above roughly $600,000 from all federal transfer taxes, with the largest benefits flowing to the biggest estates. The lost revenue would be covered by other taxpayers or larger deficits.

industries.industry: Estate planning lawyers and wealth advisors
industries.note: The bill's findings acknowledge that 'estate planning' and tax-avoidance mechanisms are a major industry built around these taxes; repeal would shrink it. This cost is borne by a professional service, not the public.

The bill's findings claim estate taxes force some family businesses and farms to liquidate to pay the tax bill. In practice, generous exemptions meant only larger estates owed the tax, so full repeal overreaches for this stated goal.
